article_title: Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation
citation: Siddhanth Sridhar, Shreya Chaurasia, Baddela Sai Yaswantha Reddy, Deepak Parmar, and Dr. Shylaja S S. (2026). Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14408
title: Multilingual synchronized narration module using Google Text-to-Speech
description: The voiceover component converts script dialogues into audio aligned with video segments. The article states that "Frame looping ensures precise narration-to-visual matching for instructional clarity," and TTS computes speech duration with text segmentation to time audio to specific scenes. It supports multilingual synthesis and translation (e.g., English to Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu) using Google Translate and gTTS to generate MP3 audio compatible across platforms.
requirements: Scene text file from the RAG stage as narration input
Speech-duration computation and text segmentation for scene-level timing
constraints: Synchronization relies on looping scenes to match narration length rather than generating visuals to fit audio
target_learners: multilingual learners, including speakers of Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, and Telugu
target_learning_goals: accessible, narrated multimedia explanations synchronized with visuals
examples: The system supports translation-based generation, e.g., English to Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, producing MP3 audio across platforms
key_sources: Siddhanth Sridhar, Shreya Chaurasia, Baddela Sai Yaswantha Reddy, Deepak Parmar, and Dr. Shylaja S S. (2026). Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14408

article_title: Gynaecology Teaching Associates in Medical Education-A Scoping Review.
citation: Kelly Caitlin, Bell Emily, Brown Megan E. L., Stelling Heidi. (2026). Gynaecology Teaching Associates in Medical Education—A Scoping Review. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70460
title: Four-domain conceptual framework of GTA programmes: educational outcomes at the core, intersecting with ethics, finance, and representation/standardisation, all shaping implementation
description: The review's conceptual framework organises the GTA literature into four interrelated domains: educational outcomes, finance, ethical considerations, and representation and standardisation. Educational outcomes sit at the core, intersecting with the three surrounding domains, while an outer box represents factors directly influencing implementation; ethics and finance extend most explicitly into this implementation space. The framework is presented in Figure 1 and summarised in Table 2, which maps barriers and enablers by factor.
requirements: The framework is a mapping of the existing GTA literature as synthesised inductively from 83 included sources via thematic synthesis.
constraints: As a scoping review, the aim was to map the literature rather than appraise effectiveness, so conclusions about impact should be interpreted cautiously.
target_learners: undergraduate medical students learning pelvic examination
examples: Figure 1 positions educational outcomes at the centre of the GTA literature with ethics, finance and standardisation intersecting it and feeding into implementation factors.
key_sources: Kelly Caitlin, Bell Emily, Brown Megan E. L., Stelling Heidi. (2026). Gynaecology Teaching Associates in Medical Education—A Scoping Review. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70460

article_title: Does Context Matter? Convergent and Divergent Findings in the Cross-Institutional Evaluation of Graduate Teaching Assistant Professional Development Programs.
citation: Reeves Todd D., Hake Laura E., Chen Xinnian, Frederick Jennifer, Rudenga Kristin, Ludlow Larry H., O'Connor Clare M. (2018). Does Context Matter? Convergent and Divergent Findings in the Cross-Institutional Evaluation of Graduate Teaching Assistant Professional Development Programs. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-03-0044
title: Conceptual framework for GTA professional development research and evaluation
description: The article is grounded in a framework (from Reeves et al., 2016) in which "The framework articulates three key PD program outcomes variables: GTA cognition; GTA teaching practice; and undergraduate student outcomes." These outcomes are posited to be linearly and probabilistically related: PD changes GTA cognition, which changes teaching practice, which changes student outcomes. The framework also contains three categories of contextual variables (GTA training design, institutional, and GTA characteristics) and two categories of moderators (implementation variables and GTA characteristics, invoking Dane and Schneider's adherence, exposure, and participant responsiveness concepts). The present study tests the framework's assertion that PD effects vary as a function of contextual factors such as GTA characteristics.
requirements: Multidimensional measurement of GTA cognition, teaching practice, and student outcomes to trace the posited sequential relationships
constraints: The relationships posited are probabilistic rather than wholly deterministic; teacher cognition is not always aligned with practice
target_learners: Graduate teaching assistants in introductory STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Teaching self-efficacy, teaching anxiety, pedagogical knowledge, and instructional practice
examples: The study compared three ST-infused presemester workshop programs at three universities along GTA cognition and student-rating outcome dimensions
key_sources: Reeves Todd D., Hake Laura E., Chen Xinnian, Frederick Jennifer, Rudenga Kristin, Ludlow Larry H., O'Connor Clare M. (2018). Does Context Matter? Convergent and Divergent Findings in the Cross-Institutional Evaluation of Graduate Teaching Assistant Professional Development Programs. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-03-0044

article_title: Peer Evaluation of Video Lab Reports in an Introductory Physics MOOC
citation: Shih-Yin Lin, Scott S. Douglas, John M. Aiken, Chien-Lin Liu, Edwin F. Greco, Brian D. Thoms, Marcos D. Caballero, and Michael F. Schatz. (2014). Peer Evaluation of Video Lab Reports in an Introductory Physics MOOC. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Peer+Evaluation+of+Video+Lab+Reports+in+an+Introductory+Physics+MOOC
title: Structured peer-evaluation rubric for video lab reports in the Georgia Tech physics MOOC
description: The Georgia Tech introductory physics MOOC used a structured rubric to guide peer evaluation of video lab reports, targeting "the quality of students’ communication (i.e, Items 1 and 2 in Table 1)" and the quality of students' discussion of results and physics explanation (Items 3-6). Rating options were three-point or five-point scales with printed point values, and text boxes allowed written suggestions for improvement.
requirements: The rating scales were pilot tested to make sure the rubric was easily interpreted for students.
constraints: Rubric item 4 was slightly changed in Lab 3 to fit that lab's purpose; all other rubric items remained the same across the four labs.
target_learners: students in an introductory calculus-based mechanics MOOC
target_learning_goals: evaluating communication quality and physics explanation in peers' video lab reports
examples: Students rated hidden calibration videos and peer videos on the rubric's scales and could add written suggestions in the text boxes following the rubric questions.
key_sources: Shih-Yin Lin, Scott S. Douglas, John M. Aiken, Chien-Lin Liu, Edwin F. Greco, Brian D. Thoms, Marcos D. Caballero, and Michael F. Schatz. (2014). Peer Evaluation of Video Lab Reports in an Introductory Physics MOOC. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Peer+Evaluation+of+Video+Lab+Reports+in+an+Introductory+Physics+MOOC

article_title: Peer Evaluation of Video Lab Reports in an Introductory Physics MOOC
citation: Shih-Yin Lin, Scott S. Douglas, John M. Aiken, Chien-Lin Liu, Edwin F. Greco, Brian D. Thoms, Marcos D. Caballero, and Michael F. Schatz. (2014). Peer Evaluation of Video Lab Reports in an Introductory Physics MOOC. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Peer+Evaluation+of+Video+Lab+Reports+in+an+Introductory+Physics+MOOC
title: Practice-video calibration intervention in the Fall 2013 MOOC offering
description: In the Fall 2013 offering, students were required to grade "four “practice videos” before they were allowed to evaluate their peers’ work" in each lab. These were sample lab reports from the previous offering "that spanned a wide range of qualit y in student work", and after each evaluation students were shown the instructor ratings and comments on the same video for reference.
requirements: Alignment with instructor ratings on the third and fourth practice videos counted toward one-third of the laboratory score, to incentivize students to read the instructor evaluation and reflect on how their ratings compared.
target_learners: MOOC students in an introductory calculus-based mechanics course
target_learning_goals: adopting instructor evaluative norms when judging peer lab reports
examples: Practice videos were drawn from the previous course offering and spanned a wide quality range; instructor ratings and comments were revealed after each student evaluation.
key_sources: Shih-Yin Lin, Scott S. Douglas, John M. Aiken, Chien-Lin Liu, Edwin F. Greco, Brian D. Thoms, Marcos D. Caballero, and Michael F. Schatz. (2014). article_title: Assessing a GTA professional development program
citation: Emily Alicea-Muñoz, Joan Espar Masip, Carol Subiño Sullivan, and Michael F. Schatz. (2018). Assessing a GTA professional development program. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02946
title: GTA preparation course integrating pedagogy, physics content, and professional development in an Orientation-plus-Follow-Ups structure
description: A one-semester course for first-year PhD GTAs, taught every Fall since 2013, whose goals are to help graduate students develop learner-centered teaching practices, give and receive feedback, manage classroom dynamics, and identify transferable skills. It is "structured in two parts: Orientation and Follow-Ups", with the Orientation a series of workshops comprising approximately 70% of contact hours before teaching duties, including Microteaching and Lab Simulation practice, followed by one-hour Follow-Up meetings every ~2-3 weeks during the semester. All class meetings are interactive, using think-pair-share, group discussion, and problem-solving activities.
requirements: A course instructor with significant GTA experience and involvement in PER and educational development
Classroom observations of GTAs during the semester, used with permission as discussion examples
constraints: Developed for first-year PhD GTAs in a physics school at a single institution
target_learners: first-year PhD graduate teaching assistants in physics
target_learning_goals: giving and receiving feedback on teaching
examples: Workshops cover expert-novice differences, addressing preconceptions, facilitating problem-solving, classroom management, and student motivation; Follow-Ups cover grading, midterm evaluations, and transferable skills
key_sources: Emily Alicea-Muñoz, Joan Espar Masip, Carol Subiño Sullivan, and Michael F. Schatz. (2018). Assessing a GTA professional development program. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02946

article_title: Transforming the Preparation of Physics GTAs: Curriculum Development
citation: Emily Alicea-Muñoz, Carol Subiño Sullivan, and Michael F. Schatz. (2021). Transforming the Preparation of Physics GTAs: Curriculum Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00168
title: Yearly cycle of implementation and revision guided by instructional design, Design Research, and Action Research
description: The course evolves through a yearly cycle: fall delivery with ongoing assessments and instructor observations, spring compilation of assessments and planning of revisions using GTA feedback and supervisor input, and summer crafting of the revised curriculum. The article grounds changes to the curriculum in the principles of instructional design and situates the process within Design Research and Action Research, in which feedback from the GTAs is crucial for the revision part of the process.
requirements: Instructor observations and assessments collected during the fall semester
GTA feedback on what was useful and what needs improvement
Input from GTA supervisors about changes to teaching assignments
constraints: Cycle is annual (fall implementation, spring planning, summer revision) and situated in a department with CTL partnership
target_learning_goals: effective teaching of labs and recitations
examples: Microteaching was revised in 2015 from topic-based lessons to facilitating selected introductory physics problems after GTAs requested more guidance
key_sources: Emily Alicea-Muñoz, Carol Subiño Sullivan, and Michael F. Schatz. (2021). Transforming the Preparation of Physics GTAs: Curriculum Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00168

article_title: A Comparative Analysis of Student Performance Predictions in Online Courses using Heterogeneous Knowledge Graphs
citation: Trask, T., Lytle, N., Boyle, M., Joyner, D., & Mubarak, A. (2024). A Comparative Analysis of Student Performance Predictions in Online Courses using Heterogeneous Knowledge Graphs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12153
title: GTX1301 Introduction to Python dual-modality course on EdX
description: Georgia Tech's GTX1301 Introduction to Python course offers both on-campus and online versions with the same lectures, assessments, and content delivered on the EdX platform. The course covers standard introductory computer science topics and is intended for students with zero or near-zero programming experience. It comprises 4 submodules (Fundamentals, Control structures, Data structures, Objects & Algorithms) with 442 videos, 216 ungraded exercises, 235 coding exercises, and 295 graded problems. On-campus students take it for a letter grade on a semester calendar; online learners are open-enrollment without fixed dates and pay a fee for graded assessments.
requirements: Payment from online learners for graded assessments
constraints: Online learners must pay a fee for graded problem sets and final test
Online instances divided into 4 submodules from which users could choose
target_learners: Georgia Tech undergraduates with zero or near-zero programming experience
examples: Five on-campus instances (Spring 2021 through Summer 2022, 1,607 total users) and two online instances (2021: 25,670 users; 2022: 21,346 users)
key_sources: Trask, T., Lytle, N., Boyle, M., Joyner, D., & Mubarak, A. (2024). A Comparative Analysis of Student Performance Predictions in Online Courses using Heterogeneous Knowledge Graphs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12153
